Read a key written as plain text

Source: R/textkey.R
keyFromText.Rd

Most identification keys exist only as printed text: floras, monographs, scans in the Biodiversity Heritage Library. keyFromText() reads such a key, one lead at a time (couplet, lead, text and destination), builds a dimoose key with keyFromLeads() and checks it with $validate(). parseTextKey() is the lower-level half that returns the lead table and the list of problems without building the key.

Usage

keyFromText(text, desc = NA, meta = NULL, llm = NULL, strict = FALSE, ...)

Arguments

text

The key: a file path, one string holding the whole key, or a character vector of lines. Give the key alone, without the descriptions before and after it.

desc

Title of the key. By default the first line above the first lead is used, if there is one.

meta

Key/value data frame of metadata (e.g. citation), passed to keyFromLeads().

llm

Optional function for a first pass over messy text; see the section below.

strict

If TRUE, stop when anything had to be repaired or any problem was found, instead of warning.

...

Further arguments for parseTextKey() (layout, skip).

Value

A dimoose key. attr(key, "problems") is a data frame of problems, repairs and notes (see parseTextKey()).

Details

Layouts that are recognised:

  • Bracketed keys, where the leads of a couplet stand together: 1a./1b., 1./1'. (primes), 1./1., 1/- (a dash for the second lead), 1(a)/1(b), (1)/(1), Roman numerals II., A./AA. or a./aa. lettering, and labels with a back-reference such as 3(1). (couplet 3, reached from couplet 1). The second lead may also be marked +, or carry no label at all: a new paragraph, as in many older entomological keys, or a line of its own with dot leaders under a complete lead.

  • Indented (yoked) keys, where the second lead of a couplet comes much later and a lead without a destination leads to the couplet printed under it.

  • Indented keys without any couplet numbers, as in most older floras: the leads of a couplet share an indent, and a lead ends in a name, often with its number in the flora (... long-acuminate. 1. S. nigra.). The couplets are made from the indentation and numbered in order. Plain OCR text usually loses the indentation. The couplets are then worked out from the order of the leads, which works when every couplet has exactly two leads: a lead without a name opens the next couplet, a lead with a name is followed by the second lead of the nearest couplet still lacking one. This is reported as a repair; if the leads do not pair off, the key is refused with the line where the pairing breaks. One key at a time: a second heading in the text stops the reading there.

  • Paired keys, where every lead has its own number and names its alternative in parentheses (1 (8) ... and further down 8 (1) ...). The two are put together as one couplet, named after the lower number.

  • Couplets with three or more leads, and couplets reached from several leads.

The destination is whatever follows dot leaders, a tab, a run of three or more spaces, a colon before a number (lobed: 5) or a spaced dash (a large tree -- Quercus alba): a couplet number (also go to 5, see 5, (5), > 5) or a taxon. A taxon may carry an authority, a common name (in parentheses, or in front of the scientific name) and a page number (Salix, p. 212, HEMIPTERA (Page 76), Culicidae, 96); the genus may be abbreviated (S. alba L.). These go to the Authority, CommonName and Page columns of the lead table. A number in parentheses after a name (Pinus. (7).) is taken for its page or list number, not for a couplet. Lead text may wrap over several lines, with the destination on the last one; words hyphenated at a line end are joined, and blank lines, page numbers, running heads and figure captions in between are skipped, as are footnotes. Text in two columns side by side (as pdftotext -layout gives it) is read column by column; this is reported as a repair. Markdown emphasis and tables are read as plain text.

Scanned text is repaired where that is safe: l, I or | read as 1 and O as 0 in couplet numbers, labels that lost their full stop, labels garbled beyond reading where only one couplet can be meant (V0. between 9 and 11), and destinations that lost their dot leaders (... each year. 11., ... leaves flat. Abies.). Text with two or more spaces between all words, as many scans have, is recognised, and only clearly wider gaps count as gaps there. Every repair is reported, and with strict = TRUE the function stops instead of repairing.

Nothing is dropped silently. A lead without a destination, a couplet with one lead, a destination couplet that does not exist, a destination that is probably a broken number (S for 5), a jump in the couplet numbers, a label that stands alone on its line, text that looks like a lead without a label and similar faults are reported with the line they are on. keyFromText() gives one warning that lists them and attaches the full table to the key as attr(key, "problems"). Text that was passed over (running heads, descriptions between leads) is listed there as notes.

What a scan has lost cannot be put back: a couplet number misread as another number that also exists in the key gives a wrong link without a warning, and leads whose labels the scan put in a column of their own are reported as lost, not recovered. Check a key read from a scan against the page. Not handled: keys without numbers that are not indented and have couplets of three or more leads, keys that mix letters and unnumbered leads (Gray's Manual), keys divided by section headings that stand for leads (A., *, ** in Britton & Brown), and text in more than two columns.

A first pass by a language model

For badly scanned keys, llm can be a function that takes the whole text as one string and returns either cleaned-up key text (one lead per line, in any layout above), a data frame with columns couplet, lead, text and destination, or the same as JSON (an array of leads; needs the jsonlite package). Markdown code fences around the answer are taken off. You write that function; dimoose calls no model or API itself. What comes back is not trusted: it goes through the same checks, and each lead is compared with the source, so a lead whose words or taxon do not occur in the source, a destination that is not on the lines of its lead in the source (two names swapped, a lead sent to another couplet), or a lead the model left out, is reported with the line of the source it belongs to (a lead that is not in the source at all has no such line; the message then names the line or row of the model's answer). The title is taken from the source, not from the answer. An answer that cannot be read (cut-off JSON, prose without leads, an empty table) is an error; nothing is taken from it.

See also

parseTextKey(), keyFromLeads()

Examples

# A bracketed key with dot leaders, wrapped leads and authorities
file <- system.file("extdata", "textkeys", "trees-bracketed.txt", package = "dimoose")
cat(readLines(file, n = 8), sep = "\n")
#> Key to the Broadleaf Trees of the Cottonwood Bottoms
#> 
#> 1a. Leaves opposite on the twig ........................................ 2
#> 1b. Leaves alternate on the twig ....................................... 4
#> 2a. Leaves simple, palmately lobed, the lobes sharply
#>     toothed ................... Acer glabrum Torr. (Rocky Mountain maple)
#> 2b. Leaves pinnately compound .......................................... 3
#> 3a. Leaflets 3 to 5, coarsely toothed or shallowly lobed; fruit a
trees <- keyFromText(file)
trees
#> <dimoose key> Key to the Broadleaf Trees of the Cottonwood Bottoms
#>   8 couplets, 16 leads, 9 taxa, up to 5 steps deep (3.6 on average)
trees$leads[, c("Statement", "Choice", "Next", "Taxon", "CommonName")]
#>    Statement Choice Next                                  Taxon
#> 1          1      a    2                                       
#> 2          1      b    4                                       
#> 3          2      a    -                           Acer glabrum
#> 4          2      b    3                                       
#> 5          3      a    -                           Acer negundo
#> 6          3      b    -                 Fraxinus pennsylvanica
#> 7          4      a    -                                  Salix
#> 8          4      b    5                                       
#> 9          5      a    6                                       
#> 10         5      b    7                                       
#> 11         6      a    -                      Betula papyrifera
#> 12         6      b    -                    Betula occidentalis
#> 13         7      a    -                    Populus tremuloides
#> 14         7      b    8                                       
#> 15         8      a    -                   Populus angustifolia
#> 16         8      b    - Populus balsamifera subsp. trichocarpa
#>               CommonName
#> 1                       
#> 2                       
#> 3   Rocky Mountain maple
#> 4                       
#> 5               boxelder
#> 6                       
#> 7                       
#> 8                       
#> 9                       
#> 10                      
#> 11           paper birch
#> 12           water birch
#> 13         quaking aspen
#> 14                      
#> 15 narrowleaf cottonwood
#> 16      black cottonwood

# An indented key, given as a string
conifers <- keyFromText(system.file("extdata", "textkeys", "conifers-indented.txt",
  package = "dimoose"))
conifers$toNewick()
#> [1] "(('Juniperus communis','Juniperus scopulorum')2,(('Pinus contorta','Pinus ponderosa',('Pinus flexilis','Pinus albicaulis')5)4,('Larix occidentalis',('Picea engelmannii',('Pseudotsuga menziesii','Abies lasiocarpa')8)7)6)3)1;"

# Problems are reported with their line and attached to the key
broken <- "1a. Wings present .... 2
1b. Wings absent .... Apterygota
2a. Two wings .... Diptera
2b. Four wings"
k <- suppressWarnings(keyFromText(broken, "Insects"))
attr(k, "problems")[, c("Line", "Lead", "Kind", "Message")]
#>   Line Lead    Kind
#> 1    4   2b problem
#>                                                           Message
#> 1 lead 2b has no destination (no couplet or taxon after the text)

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# A first pass by a language model. Any function(text) will do; this one
# calls a chat API and asks for one lead per line.
askModel <- function(text) {
  prompt <- paste(
    "This is a scanned identification key. Rewrite it with one lead per",
    "line as '<couplet><letter>. <text> .... <destination>'. Do not add,",
    "drop or reword leads.\n\n", text
  )
  response <- httr::POST(
    "https://api.example.com/v1/messages",
    httr::add_headers(Authorization = paste("Bearer", Sys.getenv("MODEL_API_KEY"))),
    body = list(model = "some-model", messages = list(list(role = "user", content = prompt))),
    encode = "json"
  )
  httr::content(response)$content[[1]]$text
}
key <- keyFromText("scanned-key.txt", llm = askModel)
attr(key, "problems")
} # }
